claim: The study included 121 participants undergoing clinical intracerebral evaluation with depth electrodes (SEEG) for refractory partial epilepsy.
source: The study included 121 participants (61 females, mean age: 32.5±8.7 years; 109 right-handed) undergoing clinical intracerebral evaluation with depth electrodes (stereotactic electroencephalography or SEEG, Figure 1A) for refractory partial epilepsy.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample in the Materials and methods section.

claim: At a statistical threshold of Z>3.1 (p<0.001), there were 2130 VOTC recording contacts in the gray matter and medial temporal lobe with significant face-selective activity in 118 participants.
source: At this statistical threshold, there were 2130 VOTC recording contacts in the gray matter and medial temporal lobe with significant face-selective activity in 118 participants (among 7374 contacts located in gray matter or medial temporal lobe in the VOTC of 121 participants, that is, 28.8% of all recorded contacts).
evidence: This is a direct quantitative result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Among face-selective recording contacts, 71% showed significant activity only in LF (LF+HF- contacts: 1511/2130).
source: Among face-selective recording contacts, 71% showed significant activity only in LF (LF+HF- contacts: 1511/2130; 118 participants, Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: 26.7% of face-selective contacts showed significant activity in both LF and HF signals (LF+HF+ contacts: 569/2130; 101 participants).
source: 26.7% showed significant activity in both LF and HF signals (LF+HF+ contacts: 569/2130; 101 participants).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: 2.3% of face-selective contacts showed significant activity in HF only (LF-HF+ contacts: 50/2130; 40 participants).
source: The remaining 2.3% contacts showed significant activity in HF only (LF-HF+ contacts: 50/2130; 40 participants).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: 91.9% of contacts with significant HF activity were also significant in LF.
source: This generated a strong asymmetry in contact overlap between signals, where the vast majority (91.9%) of contacts with significant HF activity were also significant in LF
evidence: This is a calculated result from the overlap analysis of LF and HF signals.

claim: Only 27.3% of contacts with significant LF activity were also significant in HF.
source: while only 27.3% of contacts with significant LF activity were also significant in HF.
evidence: This is a calculated result from the overlap analysis of LF and HF signals.

claim: The highest proportion of LF+HF+ contacts across VOTC was measured in the right latFG (61.3%).
source: For instance, the highest proportion of LF+HF+ contacts across VOTC (disregarding PHG and antPHG in which there were very few contacts) was measured in the right latFG (61.3%)
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding about regional differences in signal overlap.

claim: The lowest proportion of LF+HF+ contacts was observed in the TP and antMTG/ITG (2.5%).
source: while the lowest was observed in the TP and antMTG/ITG (2.5%, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative finding about regional differences in signal overlap.

claim: The proportion of LF+ contacts was significantly higher than HF+ contacts across the VOTC (28.1% for LF+ vs. 8.7% for HF+, p<0.0001).
source: Notably however, across the VOTC, the proportion of LF+ contacts was significantly higher than HF+ contacts (2080/7374=28.1% for LF+ vs. 644/7374=8.7% for HF+, p<0.0001, two-tailed permutation test, Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of proportions with a reported p-value.

claim: The proportions of both LF+ and HF+ contacts were larger in the right compared to the left hemisphere.
source: Overall, the proportions of both LF+ and HF+ contacts showed a gradual reduction from posterior to anterior VOTC (Figure 2C), and were larger in the right compared to the left hemisphere (LF+: RH = 31.7%, 1059/3339 vs. LH = 25.3%, 1021/4035, p<0.0001, two-tailed permutation test; HF+: RH = 9.6%, 322/3339 vs. LH = 8.0%, 322/4035, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison with reported p-values showing hemispheric differences.

claim: There was a strong correlation between the amplitudes computed in each region and hemispheres for LF and HF signals (Spearman's Rho = 0.81, 95% C.I.: [0.42–0.99]).
source: This similarity in patterns of amplitude is reflected in the strong correlation between the amplitudes computed in each region and hemispheres (Spearman's Rho = 0.81, 95% C.I.: [0.42–0.99] computed using 17 regions with more than 5 HF+ contacts, Figure 3B, Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: There was a robust correlation between amplitude maps computed in 12mm x 12mm voxels (Pearson' r on log-transformed data = 0.75, [0.71–0.78]).
source: This similarity manifests in the robust correlation computed between amplitude maps, that is, using mean amplitudes across contacts in each voxel (Pearson' r on log-transformed data = 0.75, [0.71–0.78], Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: For LF responses in LF+ contacts, face-selective amplitude was significantly larger in the right hemisphere in the latFG (p<0.01, FDR corrected).
source: This revealed that for LF responses in LF+ contacts, face-selective amplitude was significantly larger in the right hemisphere in the latFG (p<0.01, FDR corrected)
evidence: This is a statistical test result with FDR correction showing hemispheric differences.

claim: No significant interhemispheric difference was found for the HF signal in any region.
source: In contrast, no significant interhemispheric difference was found for the HF signal (all corrected ps >0.22; MTG, antFG, antMTG, AMG, HIP not tested due to insufficient number of HF+ contacts in these regions, see Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical test result showing lack of hemispheric differences for HF.

claim: The mean Z-score is overall higher for LF signal (mean across all VOTC contacts = 3.56 +/- 7.31) compared to HF signal (1.27+/-4.9).
source: This revealed two interesting observations: (1) the mean Z-score is overall higher for LF signal (mean across all VOTC contacts = 3.56 +/- 7.31, Figure 4A) compared to HF signal (1.27+/-4.9)
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of Z-scores between signals.

claim: The Z-scores for both LF and HF signals tend to decrease from posterior to anterior VOTC, with an abrupt reduction starting at around TAL coordinate Y = –40 to –30.
source: and (2) the Z-scores for both LF and HF signals tend to decrease from posterior to anterior VOTC, with an abrupt reduction starting at around TAL coordinate Y = –40 to –30 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation about spatial patterns in the data.

claim: The Pearson correlation computed between LF and HF Z-score profiles was 0.96.
source: Despite the difference in overall Z-score value across HF and LF signals, the postero-anterior profiles of Z-scores for the two signals were extremely similar (Pearson correlation: r=0.96).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation showing similarity between LF and HF Z-score profiles.

claim: The correlation between LF and HF Z-score profiles was not statistically different from the correlations within signals when using split-halves datasets.
source: In fact, the Pearson correlation computed between LF and HF Z-score profiles was not statistically different from the correlations within signals when using split-halves datasets (1000 random split-halves, two-tailed 95% CI for between = [0.9 0.96]; for within = [0.88 0.98])
evidence: This is a statistical comparison using split-half reliability analysis.

claim: After adjusting Z-score thresholds to match the number of significant LF+ and HF+ contacts (n=830), the spatial distribution and proportion maps for LF+ and HF+ contacts were extremely similar.
source: Under these conditions, the spatial distribution (Figure 4C) and proportion maps (Figure 4D) for LF+ and HF+ contacts were extremely similar, with no meaningful statistical difference in local proportion of contacts across VOTC (two-tailed permutation test, fdr-corrected at alpha = 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison after threshold adjustment showing similarity.

claim: The correlation between the two proportion maps after threshold adjustment was high (Spearman Rho = 0.890, 95% C.I. [0.86 0.91]).
source: This was reflected in the high correlation between the two proportion maps (Spearman Rho = 0.890, 95% C.I. [0.86 0.91]; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation with confidence intervals.

claim: The lower Z-score for HF compared to LF is driven by a smaller face-selective signal, and not by a higher noise for HF.
source: This indicates that the lower Z-score for HF compared to LF is driven by a smaller face-selective signal, and not by a higher noise for HF.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the signal and noise decomposition analysis.

claim: The mean face-selective signal amplitude within the ATL was 72% (LF) and 92% (HF) smaller than in the PTL.
source: This revealed that the mean face-selective signal amplitude within the ATL was 72% (LF) and 92% (HF) smaller than in the PTL (middle plot).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of signal amplitudes across regions.

claim: The noise in the ATL was only 10% larger (LF) or of equal magnitude (HF) than in the PTL.
source: In contrast, the noise in the ATL was only 10% larger (LF) or of equal magnitude (HF) than in the PTL (right plot).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of noise levels across regions.

claim: The lower Z-scores in ATL are mostly driven by a smaller face-selective signal amplitude in this region compared to the posterior VOTC.
source: This indicates that the lower Z-scores in ATL are mostly driven by a smaller face-selective signal amplitude in this region compared to the posterior VOTC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the signal and noise analysis in different regions.

claim: A large proportion of electrode arrays exhibited highly similar local amplitude profiles for LF and HF signals (median Pearson correlation coefficient across 215 electrode arrays = 0.69).
source: This revealed that despite the much larger number of significant contacts for LF compared to HF at the threshold of Z>3.1 (Figure 2A, Table 1), a large proportion of electrode arrays exhibited highly similar local amplitude profiles for LF and HF signals (Figure 5A and B; median Pearson correlation coefficient across 215 electrode arrays = 0.69).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of correlations within electrode arrays.

claim: For 77% of the electrode arrays, the maximum amplitude in both signals were either measured on the very same contact (48% of electrodes) or in the directly adjacent contacts spaced 3.5 mm apart (29% of electrodes).
source: In addition, as shown on Figure 5C, for 77% of the electrode arrays, the maximum amplitude in both signals where either measured on the very same contact (48% of electrodes) or in the directly adjacent contacts spaced 3.5 mm apart (29% of electrodes).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the spatial co-localization of peak amplitudes.

claim: The size of clusters of contiguous significant face-selective contacts was significantly larger for LF than for HF (mean +/-std = 3.83+/-2.66 contacts vs. 2.29+/-1.58 contacts for LF and HF respectively, p<0.0001).
source: As expected, the size of these clusters was significantly larger for LF than for HF (mean +/-std = 3.83+/-2.66 contacts vs. 2.29+/-1.58 contacts for LF and HF respectively, p<0.0001, two-tailed permutation test; that is, 13.4 mm vs. 8.0 mm for LF and HF)
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of cluster sizes with a p-value.

claim: Across regions, the average spatial extent at half-range ranged from 2.3 to 3.0 mm for LF signal and from 1.9 to 3.4 mm for HF signal.
source: Across regions, the average spatial extent at half-range ranged from 2.3 to 3.0 mm for LF signal and from 1.9 to 3.4 mm for HF signal (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about spatial extent based on amplitude decay analysis.

claim: The difference in half-range spatial extent between LF and HF was slightly but significantly larger in the left ATL (3.0 vs 2.3 mm for LF and HF respectively, p<0.005, two-tailed permutation test, fdr-corrected).
source: The difference in half-range spatial extent between LF and HF was therefore minimal, with LF being slightly but significantly larger in the left ATL (3.0 vs 2.3 mm for LF and HF respectively, p<0.005, two-tailed permutation test, fdr-corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison with FDR correction.

claim: For other regions, differences in spatial extent were not significantly different from each other (−0.5 to 0.5 mm, all ps >0.27).
source: For other regions, differences in spatial extent were not significantly different from each other (−0.5 to 0.5 mm, all ps >0.27).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison showing lack of significant differences.

claim: There was a strong relationship between LF and HF face-selective amplitudes when considering responses across the VOTC (Pearson's r on log-transformed amplitudes across 569 contacts: 0.59 [0.53–0.64], p<0.001).
source: This revealed a strong relationship when considering responses across the VOTC (Pearson's r on log-transformed amplitudes across 569 contacts: 0.59 [0.53–0.64], p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation with confidence intervals and p-value.

claim: The highest correlations between LF and HF amplitudes were found in the posterior VOTC, with local peaks in the right latFG and VMO (r~=0.8–0.9).
source: Mapping Pearson correlations in Talairach space across the VOTC (Figure 6A) revealed that the highest correlations were found in the posterior VOTC, with local peaks in the right latFG and VMO (r~=0.8–0.9)
evidence: This is a spatial mapping of correlations showing regional variations.

claim: The correlation between LF and HF signals was similar in the OCC (Pearson's r on log-transformed amplitudes: 0.63 [0.5–0.73]) and PTL (Pearson's r: 0.68 [0.61–0.75]) but slightly lower in the ATL (Pearson's r: 0.45 [0.32–0.58]).
source: This revealed similar correlations in the OCC (Pearson's r on log-transformed amplitudes: 0.63 [0.5–0.73]) and PTL (Pearson's r: 0.68 [0.61–0.75]) but a slightly lower LF-HF correlation in the ATL (Pearson's r: 0.45 [0.32–0.58]; OCC vs ATL: p=0.031; PTL vs. ATL: p<0.001, two-tailed percentile bootstrap).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of correlations across regions with p-values.

claim: Within the PTL, the correlation between LF and HF signals was much stronger in the latFG (Pearson's r: 0.73 [0.63–0.80]) than in the medFG (Pearson's r: 0.42 [0.25–0.58]).
source: Interestingly, within the PTL, the correlation between LF and HF signals was much stronger in the latFG (Pearson's r: 0.73 [0.63–0.80], log-transformed data) than in the medFG (Pearson's r: 0.42 [0.25–0.58]).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of correlations within subregions.

claim: The maximum expected correlation (MEC) at the level of the whole VOTC was 0.88, 99% CI: [0.85–0.91].
source: The MEC (averaged across LF and HF) at the level of the whole VOTC was 0.88, 99% CI: [0.85–0.91].
evidence: This is a calculated estimate of maximum expected correlation based on noise analysis.

claim: The correlation between LF and HF signals reaches 71%, 99% CI: [67-76]% of the maximum expected correlation in the VOTC dataset.
source: This means that the correlation between LF and HF signals reaches 71%, 99% CI: [67-76]% ( ratio of the actual LF vs. HF correlation to the MEC: 0.59/0.83) of the maximum expected correlation in this dataset.
evidence: This is a calculated ratio comparing actual to maximum expected correlation.

claim: The face-selectivity indices were virtually identical between LF and HF signals, with no significant difference between signals in any main VOTC region (range of FSI difference: –0.023–0.041; all ps >0.6, fdr-corrected).
source: Comparing LF to HF FSI for each main VOTC region and hemisphere (Figure 7A) revealed no significant difference between signals (range of FSI difference: –0.023–0.041; all ps >0.6, fdr-corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison showing no significant differences.

claim: Selectivity indices increased from posterior VOTC / OCC (LF = 0.64, 99% CI: [0.60–0.69]; HF = 0.62 [0.56–0.67]) to anterior VOTC / ATL (LF = 0.87 [0.85–0.89] and HF = 0.86 [0.84–0.89]).
source: Second, selectivity indices increased from posterior VOTC / OCC (LF = 0.64, 99% confidence interval: [0.60–0.69]; HF = 0.62 [0.56–0.67]) to anterior VOTC / ATL (LF = 0.87 [0.85–0.89] and HF = 0.86 [0.84–0.89]) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about spatial gradients in face-selectivity.

claim: The face-selectivity indices were larger in the right than in the left hemisphere in OCC (left = 0.57 [0.5–0.64] vs. right = 0.71 [0.65–0.76], p<0.005, fdr-corrected) and PTL (left = 0.74 [0.7–0.77] vs. right = 0.80 [0.76–0.83], p<0.005).
source: Third, the face-selectivity indices were larger in the right than in the left hemisphere in OCC (averaging LF and HF: left = 0.57 [0.5–0.64] vs. right = 0.71 [0.65–0.76], p<0.005, fdr-corrected) and PTL (left = 0.74 [0.7–0.77] vs. right = 0.80 [0.76–0.83], p<0.005) regions.
evidence: This is a statistical comparison showing hemispheric differences with FDR correction.

claim: In the ATL, the FSI was slightly larger in the left hemisphere (left = 0.89 [0.87–0.91] vs. right = 0.85 [0.82–0.88], p<0.01).
source: In the ATL, the FSI was slightly larger in the left hemisphere (left = 0.89 [0.87–0.91] vs. right = 0.85 [0.82–0.88], p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison showing hemispheric differences in the ATL.

claim: Both LF and HF signals started to deviate from baseline at around the same latency (LF: 79ms, 95% CI: [58 - 101] ms and HF: 91ms, [82 - 103] ms).
source: As shown in Figure 8B, both signals started to deviate from baseline at around the same latency (LF: 79ms, 95% confidence interval: [58 - 101] ms and HF: 91ms, [82 - 103] ms)
evidence: This is a quantitative timing analysis with confidence intervals.

claim: The LF signal significantly rose above baseline slightly later than HF (102ms, [96 - 108] ms vs. 77ms, [75 - 81] ms for LF and HF respectively).
source: although the LF signal significantly rose above baseline slightly later than HF (102ms, [96 - 108] ms vs. 77ms, [75 - 81] ms for LF and HF respectively) due to higher across-trial standard deviation for LF.
evidence: This is a quantitative timing comparison with confidence intervals.

claim: The response duration was longer for LF, returning to baseline level at 639ms (95% CI: [637 641]), compared to HF signal which returned to baseline level at 409 ms [402 - 430].
source: In addition, the response duration was longer for LF, returning to baseline level at 639ms (95% confidence interval: [637 641]), compared to HF signal which returned to baseline level at 409 ms [402 - 430].
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of response durations with confidence intervals.

claim: There was a highly significant correlation between LF and HF onset latencies (Pearson's r=0.48, p<0.001, 99% CI: [0.23 0.67]).
source: This revealed a highly significant correlation between LF and HF onset latencies (Pearson's r=0.48, p<0.001, 99% CI: [0.23 0.67], Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a statistical correlation with p-value and confidence intervals.

claim: The Pearson correlation between LF and HF onset latencies was higher when including only contacts with higher Z-score (r=0.63 for the 30 contacts with highest Z-score and peaked at r=0.68 for the 16 contacts with highest Z-scores).
source: Hence, the correlation across latencies was higher when including only contacts with higher Z-score. For instance, Pearson's r was 0.63 when only including the 30 contacts with highest Z-score and peaked at r=0.68 for the 16 contacts with highest Z-scores.
evidence: This is an analysis showing how correlation varies with signal quality.

claim: LF and HF display highly similar spatial, functional, and timing properties.
source: While LF face-selective activity has higher SNR across the VOTC, leading to a larger number of significant electrode contacts especially in the anterior temporal lobe, LF and HF display highly similar spatial, functional, and timing properties.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Abstract synthesizing multiple findings.

claim: LF and HF have nearly identical spatial distribution and local spatial extent at equal SNR.
source: Specifically, and contrary to a widespread assumption, our results point to nearly identical spatial distribution and local spatial extent of LF and HF activity at equal SNR.
evidence: This is a key conclusion stated in the Abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: HF is thought to be more focal and closely related to spiking activity.
source: While most current studies rely exclusively on HF, thought to be more focal and closely related to spiking activity, the relationship between HF and LF signals is unclear, especially in human associative cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the field.

claim: HF appears to be more correlated with BOLD activity as recorded with fMRI than LF.
source: Although early work focused exclusively on characterizing LF activity, the neuroscientific community has now largely shifted its interest to HF signals, which are thought to reflect population-level neuronal firing (Miller et al., 2007; Nir et al., 2007; Ray et al., 2008) and to be more correlated with blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) activity as recorded with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) (Mukamel et al., 2005; Hermes et al., 2012; Winawer et al., 2013; Jacques et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between HF and BOLD supported by citations.

claim: HF is typically assumed to reflect more local neural activity than LF.
source: Compared to low frequency signals, HF also appears to be more straightforward to characterize the time-course of sensory-motor and cognitive processes (i.e. avoiding the issue of varying polarity and morphology of ERP responses), may be more selective to specific stimuli (Rangarajan et al., 2014), and is typically assumed to reflect more local neural activity (Crone et al., 1998; Miller et al., 2007; Hermes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing assumption in the field supported by citations.

claim: The neuroscientific community has largely shifted its interest from LF to HF signals.
source: Although early work focused exclusively on characterizing LF activity, the neuroscientific community has now largely shifted its interest to HF signals
evidence: This is a statement about trends in the field.

claim: Most previous intracranial EEG studies focusing on HF reported no or little face-selective ATL activity.
source: As a matter of fact, most previous intracranial EEG studies focusing on HF reported no or little face-selective ATL activity (e.g. Sanada et al., 2021; Schrouff et al., 2020; Jacques et al., 2016b; Davidesco et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2017; Norman et al., 2019; Rangarajan et al., 2014; Kadipasaoglu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about previous literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is the exploration of LF signal in intracranial electrophysiology that has truly brought forward the ATL as a major face-selective region.
source: Thus, overall, it is fair to say that it is the exploration of LF signal in intracranial electrophysiology that has truly brought forward the ATL as a major face-selective region, especially the antFG and adjacent sulci (Jonas et al., 2016; Hagen et al., 2020; Jacques et al., 2020; Volfart et al., 2022; the current study).
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the contribution of LF studies supported by citations.

claim: The disproportionately lower proportion of HF+ responses in the ATL results mostly from a quantitative difference between LF and HF rather than a qualitative difference.
source: Thus, according to these findings, the disproportionately lower proportion of HF+ responses in the ATL results mostly from a quantitative difference between LF and HF.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about ATL responses.

claim: The lower face-selective signal amplitude in the ATL may relate to physiological properties of the cortex in this region, potentially generating weak population-level neural activity.
source: Future intracranial human recording studies will have to determine whether the lower face-selective signal amplitude in the ATL relates to physiological properties of the cortex in this region, potentially generating weak population-level neural activity, and if it can be increased by using more suitable stimuli (e.g. familiar faces linked to semantic information; Collins and Olson, 2014; Rice et al., 2018) for this region.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential explanations for the findings.

claim: The assumption that HF is more focal than LF rests on findings from studies that quantified spatial extent by counting the number of recording sites with significant responses.
source: In human intracranial recordings, it is generally assumed that HF signals reflect a more local neural activity than LF signals and hence provide higher spatial resolution (Crone et al., 1998; Crone et al., 2006; Pfurtscheller et al., 2003; Miller et al., 2007; Hermes et al., 2012; Lachaux et al., 2012). However, this assumption rests on findings from studies that have quantified the spatial extent by counting the number of recording sites with significant responses for LF and for HF (Miller et al., 2007; Crone et al., 1998; Pfurtscheller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a critical statement about the methodological basis of a prevailing assumption.

claim: Counting significant responses confounds the quantification of spatial spread of the signal and the quantification of the spatial extent of the cortical source.
source: In other words, counting significant responses confounds the quantification of spatial spread or 'reach' of the signal, and the quantification of the spatial extent of the cortical source.
evidence: This is a methodological critique explaining a potential confound.

claim: The lack of a difference in the amplitude decay function between LF and HF suggests a comparable cortical area generating the two signals.
source: Overall, this lack of a difference in the amplitude decay function suggests a comparable cortical area generating the two signals, at least at the scale of our recordings, and a comparable source geometry (i.e., location, orientation and number of sources and sinks in the cortical layers, Herreras, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial extent findings.

claim: The view that HF signal is more focal than LF signal is partly inspired by the finding that HF signal measured with micro-electrodes correlates with neuronal spiking activity.
source: Several additional factors may explain the discrepancy between our and previous findings from human intracranial recordings in terms of relative spatial extent of HF and LF. First, the view that the HF signal is more focal than the LF signal is partly inspired by the finding that the HF signal measured with micro-electrodes correlates with neuronal spiking activity (Manning et al., 2009; Ray et al., 2008; Nir et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an explanation of the origin of a prevailing view supported by citations.

claim: Spiking activity and HF do not always correlate, especially in superficial layers close to the cortical surface.
source: However, spiking activity and HF do not always correlate, especially in superficial layers close to the cortical surface (Leszczyński et al., 2020) where macro-electrode HF is typically measured as in the ECoG studies that have highlighted a more focal activity for HF compared to LF (Miller et al., 2007; Crone et al., 1998; Pfurtscheller et al., 2003; Hermes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between spiking and HF supported by a citation.

claim: The spatial properties of HF measured with micro-electrodes may not translate to HF signal measured with macro-electrodes.
source: In other words, the spatial properties of HF measured with micro-electrodes may not translate to HF signal measured with macro-electrodes.
evidence: This is an inference about the generalizability of findings across recording methods.

claim: Both neuronal density and myelination are substantially lower in associative cortices than in primary cortices in primates.
source: Moreover, by recording higher-order category-selective activity, we measured activity confined to associative areas. Both neuronal density (Collins et al., 2010; Turner et al., 2016) and myelination (Bryant and Preuss, 2018) are substantially lower in associative cortices than in primary cortices in primates
evidence: This is a statement about cortical properties supported by citations.

claim: These cortical factors may contribute to the lack of spatial extent difference between HF and LF observed in this study compared to previous reports.
source: and these factors may thus contribute to the lack of spatial extent difference between HF and LF observed here as compared to previous reports.
evidence: This is an inference about factors contributing to the study's findings.

claim: Previous studies compared the spatial properties of an increase in HF amplitude to the spatial properties of a decrease of LF amplitude in the alpha and beta frequency ranges.
source: Third, previous studies compared the spatial properties of an increase (relative to baseline) in HF amplitude to the spatial properties of a decrease (i.e. event-related desynchronization) of LF amplitude in the alpha and beta frequency ranges (Crone et al., 1998; Pfurtscheller et al., 2003; Miller et al., 2007; Hermes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology of previous studies supported by citations.

claim: The comparison between increases and decreases in neural signals may be unwarranted due to likely different mechanisms involved.
source: This comparison may be unwarranted due to likely different mechanisms, brain networks and cortical layers involved in generating neuronal increases and decreases (e.g. input vs. modulatory signal, Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological critique supported by citations.

claim: The correlations between LF and HF signals are not at ceiling and there were slight offsets in the location of maximum amplitude across signals along electrode arrays.
source: We acknowledge that the correlations found here are not at ceiling and that there were also slight offsets in the location of maximum amplitude across signals along electrode arrays (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations in the functional correspondence between signals.

claim: LF and HF signals have distinct neurophysiological origins that are not yet fully understood.
source: For instance, although both signals involve post-synaptic (i.e. dentritic) neural events, they nevertheless have distinct neurophysiological origins (that are not yet fully understood; see Buzsáki et al., 2012; Leszczyński et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a statement about the neurophysiological basis of the signals supported by citations.

claim: The difference in neurophysiological origins is manifested as the difference in the frequency range at which these signals are most prevalent and the difference of phase-locking relative to the stimulation.
source: that are manifested in the current study as the difference in the frequency range at which these signals are most prevalent, or the difference of phase-locking relative to the stimulation between LF signals (here mostly phase-locked) and HF signals (mostly non phase-locked, Lachaux et al., 2005; Winawer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an explanation of how neurophysiological differences manifest in the signals.

claim: Both HF and LF signals, when measured in VOTC, have been shown to be roughly equivalent in predicting the presentation time and category of a stimulus.
source: Both signals, when measured in VOTC, have been shown to be roughly equivalent in predicting the presentation time and category of a stimulus (face or house), although slightly higher performance were obtained when combining the signals, indicating that they contain a slight amount of complementary information (Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the functional value of the signals supported by a citation.

claim: HF receptive fields derived from visual retinotopic mapping are slightly more similar to size and locations of phosphenes induced by electrical stimulation than LF.
source: For instance, Winawer and Parvizi, 2016 found that HF receptive fields derived from visual retinotopic mapping are slightly more similar to size and locations of phosphenes induced by electrical stimulation, although a combination of signals was not tested.
evidence: This is a statement about a previous finding supported by a citation.

claim: Conscious face distortions evoked by ECoG electrical stimulation over the middle FG could be predicted by the degree of face-selectivity measured in HF but not in LF.
source: In addition, Rangarajan et al., 2014 reported that conscious face distortions evoked by ECoG electrical stimulation over the middle FG could be predicted by the degree of face-selectivity measured in HF but not in LF, suggesting a higher functional value of HF than LF signals.
evidence: This is a statement about a previous finding supported by a citation.

claim: Objective transient face identity recognition impairments during intracerebral electrical stimulation appear to be highly related to LF indexes of face-selectivity.
source: Nevertheless, objective transient face identity recognition impairments during intracerebral electrical stimulation appear to be highly related to LF indexes of face-selectivity (Jonas et al., 2012; Jonas et al., 2015; see also Jonas et al., 2018; Volfart et al., 2022 for similar relationships between LF and HF signals of face-selectivity and sensitivity to individual faces and the transient effect of intracerebral stimulation on behavior).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between LF and behavioral effects supported by citations.

claim: The study recorded from a large cortical surface ranging from the occipital to the temporal poles and encompassing various types of cortices.
source: First, we recorded from a large cortical surface (i.e. the VOTC), ranging from the occipital to the temporal poles and encompassing various types of cortices, architectonics, and cognitive systems: primary and associative cortices, unimodal visual (posterior VOTC) and multimodal semantic (ATL) cortices, neocortex and medial temporal structures (e.g. hippocampus).
evidence: This is a description of the study's sampling approach.

claim: The findings are likely to largely apply to other, unsampled brain regions given the diversity of cortices sampled.
source: Given this diversity, our findings are likely to largely apply to other, unsampled brain regions.
evidence: This is an inference about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The use of natural images of faces and contrasted nonface object categories increases the ecological validity of the paradigm.
source: Moreover, the use of natural images of such stimuli, as well as the contrasted nonface object categories, increase the ecological validity of our paradigm.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological strength of the study.

claim: SEEG recordings are sampled from all cortical layers and a wide range of anatomical structures and cortical geometries.
source: Third, while ECoG mainly records activity from gyri and superficial cortical layers, SEEG (i.e. intracerebral) recordings, which are increasingly being used in the neuroscientific community, are sampled from all cortical layers and a wide range of anatomical structures and cortical geometries (sulci, gyri, deep structures, etc.), a diversity that increases generalizability of our findings.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of SEEG recordings.

claim: The relatively low spatial resolution of SEEG and ECoG makes it very unlikely that they would reveal different patterns of LF-HF functional correspondence.
source: Despite this noticeable difference, the relatively low spatial resolution of these 2 recording methods (i.e., several millimeters) and size of recording sites (~2 mm) compared to the average cortical thickness (~2–3 mm) makes it very unlikely that SEEG and ECoG would reveal different patterns of LF-HF functional correspondence.
evidence: This is an inference about the comparability of SEEG and ECoG findings.

claim: Frequency-tagging provides objectivity of response identification and quantification, and similarity across analysis pipelines for LF and HF.
source: Finally, we relied on a well-validated frequency-tagging stimulation approach, which provides objectivity of response identification and quantification, and similarity across analysis pipelines for LF and HF.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological advantages of the approach.

claim: Frequency-tagged neural responses are independent of temporal predictability and qualitatively similar across a well-defined suitable frequency range.
source: In addition, frequency-tagged neural responses as used in the present paradigm with natural variable images are independent of temporal predictability (i.e. strictly identical to responses obtained in a nonperiodic presentation mode; Quek and Rossion, 2017) and qualitatively similar across a well-defined suitable frequency range (Retter and Rossion, 2016; Retter et al., 2020), further increasing their generalizability.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of frequency-tagged responses supported by citations.

claim: The observations indicate that neglecting LF signals in favor of HF activity comes at a cost in terms of identification and characterization of regions associated with low HF signal such as the VATL.
source: Moreover, our observations indicate that neglecting LF signals in favor of HF activity comes at a cost in terms of identification and characterization of regions associated with low HF signal such as the VATL, which plays a key role in various higher order brain function including semantic cognition (Lambon Ralph et al., 2010; Persichetti et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings supported by citations.

claim: The observations reestablish the informative value of LF iEEG to understand human brain function.
source: These observations go a long way towards clarifying the relationship between the two main iEEG signals and reestablish the informative value of LF iEEG to understand human brain function.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the Abstract about the implications of the findings.

claim: The observations reestablish the high value of LF in mapping neural activity in human associative cortex with iEEG.
source: Altogether, these observations, which are discussed more specifically below, re-establish the high value of LF in mapping neural activity in human associative cortex with iEEG.
evidence: This is a concluding statement in the Discussion about the value of LF signals.

claim: A total of 856 electrode arrays were implanted in the VOTC of the 121 participants, containing 9703 individual recording contacts.
source: A total of 856 electrode arrays were implanted in the VOTC of the 121 participants. These electrodes contained 9703 individual recording contacts in the VOTC (i.e., in the gray/white matter or medial temporal lobe-MTL; 5316 contacts in the left hemisphere, 4387 in the right hemisphere).
evidence: This is a description of the recording setup and sample size.

claim: Each 0.8 mm diameter intracerebral electrode contains 5–15 independent recording contacts of 2 mm in length separated by 1.5 mm from edge to edge.
source: Each 0.8 mm diameter intracerebral electrode contains 5–15 independent recording contacts of 2 mm in length separated by 1.5 mm from edge to edge (Figure 1A, for details about the electrode implantation procedure, see Salado et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the electrode specifications.

claim: Intracerebral EEG was sampled at either 500 or 512 Hz and referenced to either a midline prefrontal scalp electrode (FPz, 94 participants) or an intracerebral contact in the white matter (in 27 participants).
source: Intracerebral EEG was sampled at either 500 or 512 Hz and referenced to either a midline prefrontal scalp electrode (FPz, 94 participants) or an intracerebral contact in the white matter (in 27 participants).
evidence: This is a description of the recording parameters.

claim: SEEG signal at each recording contact was re-referenced offline to bipolar reference to limit dependencies between neighboring contacts.
source: SEEG signal at each recording contact was re-referenced offline to bipolar reference to limit dependencies between neighboring contacts (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the signal processing method supported by a citation.

claim: A contact was considered as showing a face-selective response if the Z-score at the frequency bin of face stimulation exceeded 3.1 (i.e. p<0.001 one-tailed).
source: A contact was considered as showing a face-selective response if the Z-score at the frequency bin of face stimulation exceeded 3.1 (i.e. p<0.001 one-tailed: signal >noise).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical threshold used for significance.

claim: The frequency bandwidth of the lowest wavelet (5 cycles at 40 Hz) was 20 Hz (full width at half maximum).
source: The frequency bandwidth of the lowest wavelet (5 cycles at 40 Hz) was 20 Hz (full width at half maximum).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the wavelet analysis.

claim: The lower boundary of the frequency bandwidth for the HF signal was 30 Hz (i.e. 40 – 20/2 Hz).
source: Using these parameters, the lower boundary of the frequency bandwidth for the HF signal was 30 Hz (i.e. 40 – 20/2 Hz).
evidence: This is a calculated specification of the HF frequency range.

claim: The highest significant harmonic of face-selective response in the FPVS experiment was 22.8 Hz.
source: This was well above the highest significant harmonic of face-selective response in the FPVS experiment which was 22.8 Hz (defined as the harmonic of the 1.2 Hz face frequency where, at the group level, the number of recording contacts with a significant response was not higher than the number of significant contacts detected for noise in bins surrounding harmonics of the face frequency).
evidence: This is a data-driven determination of the highest significant harmonic.

claim: The HF signal measured in the 40–160 Hz range is not contaminated by lower frequency responses.
source: This ensures that the signal measured in the 40–160 Hz range is not contaminated by lower frequency responses.
evidence: This is an inference about the validity of the HF measurement based on the frequency parameters.

claim: All participants gave written consent to participate to the study, which was approved by the local human investigation committee (MAPCOG 2017-A03248-45).
source: All participants gave written consent to participate to the study, which was approved by the local human investigation committee (MAPCOG 2017-A03248-45).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval and informed consent.

claim: Two hundred grayscale natural images of various non-face objects and 50 grayscale natural images of faces were used.
source: Two hundred grayscale natural images of various non-face objects (from 14 non-face categories: cats, dogs, horses, birds, flowers, fruits, vegetables, houseplants, phones, chairs, cameras, dishes, guitars, lamps) and 50 grayscale natural images of faces were used (the same stimuli as in Rossion et al., 2015; Jonas et al., 2016; Hagen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus set.

claim: Global images were equalized for mean pixel luminance and contrast, but low-level visual cues associated with the faces and visual objects remained highly variable.
source: Global images were equalized for mean pixel luminance and contrast, but low-level visual cues associated with the faces and visual objects remained highly variable, naturally eliminating the systematic contribution of low-level visual cues to the recorded face-selective neural responses (Rossion et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of stimulus properties and their implications supported by citations.

claim: A stimulation sequence lasted 70 s: 66 s of stimulation at full-contrast flanked by 2 s of fade-in and fade-out.
source: A stimulation sequence lasted 70 s: 66 s of stimulation at full-contrast flanked by 2 s of fade-in and fade-out, where contrast gradually increased or decreased, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the stimulation protocol.

claim: Participants were instructed to fixate a small black cross and to detect brief color-changes of this fixation-cross.
source: During a sequence, participants were instructed to fixate a small black cross which was presented continuously at the center of the stimuli and to detect brief (500ms) color-changes (black to red) of this fixation-cross.
evidence: This is a description of the task instructions.

claim: Among the 121 participants, the number of sequences viewed ranged from 2 to 8 or more.
source: Among the 121 participants, participants viewed either 2 sequences (65 participants), 3 sequences (5 participants), 4 sequences (42 participants), 5 sequences (1 participant), 6 sequences (3 participants), 8, or more sequences (5 participants).
evidence: This is a description of the variability in data collection across participants.

claim: No participant had seizures in the 2 hr preceding the recordings.
source: No participant had seizures in the 2 hr preceding the recordings.
evidence: This is a statement about participant clinical status during the study.
